title: DJI Neo 2 Review: Is the $259 Self-Flying Drone Worth It?
excerpt: A research-based DJI Neo 2 review: a 151g self-flying 4K drone with a real gimbal and obstacle sensing. Who it's for, and the one catch buyers flag.
body:
You want cinematic clips of yourself hiking, skiing, or just walking the dog, but you don't want to learn stick controls or spend $800 to get them. That gap is exactly what the DJI Neo line was built to fill, and the second-generation model tries to fix nearly everything people griped about in the first one.

This DJI Neo 2 review is research-based. GadgetDrop does not fly every product itself, so what follows pulls together the published spec sheet, figures reported by professional testers, and the patterns showing up in verified-purchase owner feedback. The goal is to tell you who should buy this drone, who shouldn't, and the one thing almost every owner mentions.

---

## What Is the DJI Neo 2?

The DJI Neo 2 is a palm-sized, self-flying camera drone that weighs 151 grams. You can literally launch it off your open hand, tell it to follow you, and it films 4K video while it flies itself. There is no mandatory remote, no goggles, and no piloting skill required for the basic modes. A phone app, a hand gesture, or a spoken preset is enough to get a usable clip.

Under the hood it carries a 12-megapixel, 1/2-inch sensor with an f/2.2 lens, shoots 4K at 60 frames per second, and adds a 4K/100fps slow-motion mode plus 2.7K vertical video for social clips. The headline upgrade over the original is a proper 2-axis mechanical gimbal instead of the first Neo's single-axis design, so footage looks steady rather than jittery. It also adds omnidirectional obstacle sensing with a forward LiDAR sensor, which is the feature that makes it hard to crash.

---

## Who Should Buy the DJI Neo 2?

This drone is for creators and casual flyers, not for aerial professionals. If you make short-form video for Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube and you want dynamic shots of yourself in motion, the Neo 2 is close to a point-and-shoot. Runners, cyclists, skaters, and parents who want a follow-cam without a learning curve are the core audience.

It also suits total beginners nervous about crashing an expensive drone into a tree. The obstacle sensing and the low 151-gram weight lower both the risk and the paperwork. Because it sits well under the 250-gram line, recreational flyers in the US skip FAA drone registration entirely, which removes one of the most annoying barriers to a first drone.

Skip it if you want long flights, professional-grade stills, or the range and manual control of a Mini-class drone. This is a lightweight companion camera, not a workhorse.

---

## Key Features That Actually Matter

- **2-axis gimbal plus stabilization:** the mechanical gimbal is the single biggest reason footage looks smooth. The original Neo leaned on a single-axis gimbal and electronic smoothing, and the difference is obvious in side-by-side clips professional testers have posted.
- **Omnidirectional obstacle sensing with forward LiDAR:** the first Neo could only see straight down. The Neo 2 watches all directions, so it dodges branches and walls while it tracks you. This is what turns "self-flying" from a gimmick into something you trust near people.
- **4K/60 and 4K/100 slow motion:** a wider f/2.2 aperture pulls in more light than the old f/2.8 lens, and the 100fps slow-motion mode from a sub-250g drone is the spec reviewers single out as genuinely impressive at this price.
- **Palm launch and gesture control:** no controller needed for the basics. You hold it up, it lifts off, and preset shots like orbit, boomerang, and follow run on their own.
- **Level 5 wind resistance and 500m range:** it holds position in gusts up to about 10.7 m/s and flies far further than the original's 50-meter tether, so it drifts and fights the breeze less.

---

## What You'll Pay

At roughly $259 for the drone-only package as of this writing, the Neo 2 sits at the very bottom of DJI's lineup and undercuts almost every other 4K drone with real obstacle avoidance. You are paying a small premium over the outgoing model for the gimbal and the all-around sensors, which are the two upgrades most worth having. The Fly More combos cost more because they bundle extra batteries, and given the flight time below, that math is worth doing. The price widget above shows where today's tracked number sits against our recorded history, so you can see whether this is a normal price or a dip before you commit.

---

## DJI Neo 2 vs. the Original Neo and HoverAir X1

The original **DJI Neo** still sells for around $159 and remains the cheapest way into a DJI drone. It shoots 4K but only at 30fps, uses a single-axis gimbal, sees obstacles only below itself, and tops out at level 4 wind resistance with a 50-meter range. Buy it only if you want the lowest possible price for close-range selfie clips and you can live with shakier footage.

The **HoverAir X1** is the main rival in the self-flying-selfie category and leans even harder into pocketable, grab-and-go simplicity. It is worth a look if fully automatic framing matters more to you than DJI's camera quality and obstacle sensing, but the Neo 2 generally wins on video specs.

If you would rather hold your camera than let it fly itself, an action cam is the other path. Our [GoPro HERO13 Black review](/posts/gopro-hero13-black-review) covers that trade-off, since a chest or helmet mount gives you unlimited "flight time" and no airspace rules to worry about.

---

## One Thing to Consider

The catch is flight time. DJI rates the battery at about 19 minutes, but that number assumes a gentle hover. Once you factor in active tracking, wind correction, and the transceiver module, professional testers and owners consistently report closer to 8 to 10 minutes of real recording per charge. That is short. It is the number-one complaint in verified-purchase feedback, and it is the reason the multi-battery combo exists. A couple of owners also note the obstacle sensing can miss glass or water, so keep it away from ponds and windows.

---

## DJI Neo 2 FAQ

**Q: Is the DJI Neo 2 worth it over the original Neo?**
For most buyers, yes. The 2-axis gimbal and omnidirectional obstacle sensing are meaningful upgrades that directly affect how usable your footage is and how safe the drone feels. The original Neo only makes sense if the roughly $100 saving matters more than smooth video.

**Q: How long does the DJI Neo 2 actually fly?**
DJI rates it near 19 minutes, but real-world recording with tracking runs closer to 8 to 10 minutes per battery according to owner and tester reports. Plan on landing to swap batteries often, and budget for a spare or the Fly More combo.

**Q: Do I need to register the DJI Neo 2 with the FAA?**
At 151 grams it falls under the 250-gram threshold, so recreational flyers in the US do not need to register it. You should still follow local rules and the FAA's recreational flying guidelines, but you skip the formal registration step.

---

## The Verdict

The DJI Neo 2 is the easiest 4K drone to recommend to a first-timer who wants hands-free clips, thanks to the gimbal, the all-around sensors, and the no-registration weight. Buy it if short flights don't scare you off, wait for the multi-battery combo if you shoot longer sessions, and step down to the original Neo only if $100 is the deciding factor.

---

If the current price in the card above sits at or near typical, this is an easy yes for casual creators. Grab an extra battery with it and the short flight time stops being a dealbreaker.
